text:
<meta>This page continues the declaration of the Venerable Sāriputta, who is defending his conduct before the Buddha after being accused by another monk of causing offense.</meta>

Just as, venerable sir, a dust-cloth <note>original: rajoharaṇaṃ</note> wipes away what is clean and wipes away what is dirty, wipes away what is smeared with excrement, wipes away what is smeared with urine, wipes away what is smeared with saliva, wipes away what is smeared with pus, and wipes away what is smeared with blood, yet the dust-cloth is not distressed or disgusted by it: even so, venerable sir, do I dwell with a mind like a dust-cloth, vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill-will. Only one who did not have mindfulness directed to the body <note>original: kāyagatā sati</note> established in the body would, having offended a fellow practitioner here, depart on a journey without making amends.

Just as, venerable sir, a boy of the <term>Caṇḍāla</term> <gloss>lowest social class, often task-bound to manual labor or waste removal</gloss> caste or a girl of the <term>Caṇḍāla</term> caste, with a basket in hand and dressed in rags, enters a village or a town with a humble heart: even so, venerable sir, do I dwell with a mind like a <term>Caṇḍāla</term> boy, vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill-will. Only one who did not have mindfulness directed to the body established in the body would, having offended a fellow practitioner here, depart on a journey without making amends.

Just as, venerable sir, a bull with its horns cut off, gentle, well-tamed, and well-trained, as it wanders from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads, does not harm anything with its feet or its horns: even so, venerable sir, do I dwell with a mind like a bull with its horns cut off, vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill-will. Only one who did not have mindfulness directed to the body established in the body would, having offended a fellow practitioner here, depart on a journey without making amends.

Just as, venerable sir, a woman or a man, young and youthful, fond of ornaments, having bathed their head, <note>would be disgusted if the carcass of a snake</note> <margin>the text breaks off here to describe the reaction to a carcass</margin> with the carcass of a snake or...

<summary>Sāriputta uses a series of metaphors—a dust-cloth, a low-caste child, and a de-horned bull—to demonstrate his humility and lack of ego when accused of an offense. He emphasizes that one who maintains mindfulness of the body cannot harbor ill-will or arrogance toward others.</summary>

<keywords>Sāriputta, humility, mindfulness of the body, metaphors, Caṇḍāla, monastic discipline, non-harming, Aṅguttara Nikāya</keywords>
